blocks.text: Most eDiscovery work happens in web-based interfaces. When you open a review platform in Chrome, you are essentially loading a massive database of ESI. Chrome handles this well, but it consumes significant memory. To keep things stable, avoid keeping dozens of tabs open for unrelated tasks. Create a dedicated Chrome Profile for every active case. Go to Menu > Profile icon > Add to create a new one. This keeps your cookies and cache separate for each client. It also prevents cross-contamination of authentication sessions.

Speed is your best friend when reviewing thousands of records. Stop reaching for your mouse to switch tabs or refresh pages. Use ⌘ + T to open a new tab and ⌘ + L to jump straight to the address bar. If you need to jump between open tabs, use ⌘ + Option + Right Arrow. These small movements add up over an eight-hour shift. If you find yourself clicking the same buttons repeatedly, check if your review platform supports custom keyboard mapping.

You will eventually hit a wall where a document fails to load or the viewer crashes. This is often a cache issue. Instead of clearing everything, you can clear site data for one website in Chrome. Navigate to the specific site, click the lock icon in the address bar, and select Site settings. From there, you can clear data without logging yourself out of every other platform. If you see the Aw, Snap error, it is usually a memory issue. Close your other resource-heavy tabs or restart the browser.

Lazur sits in your Mac notch and listens while you hold Option + Command. You do not need to hunt for settings or remember complex paths. If you need to clear your cache, just ask Lazur to guide you. It will point at the correct menu items one by one. This keeps your hands on the keyboard and your eyes on the document review grid.

When you have a long list of document IDs to research, do not copy and paste them one by one. Use Lazur to dictate notes or search queries directly into your review platform's search bar. It saves you from the repetitive strain of switching windows.
blocks.title: Speed up your data entry

blocks.text: Your desktop should be an extension of your review workflow. Use the Dock for your most used apps. If you frequently access a specific web-based review portal, you can add a website to the Dock in Chrome. It makes that platform feel like a native Mac app. Keep your downloads folder clean as well. eDiscovery specialists often accumulate thousands of CSV files and exported reports. Create a folder system by case name and date to avoid the 34% of professionals who waste hours just finding files.

Security is non-negotiable when handling legal data. Chrome offers several layers of protection. Always ensure you are signed into the correct corporate profile. Block third-party cookies in Chrome if your firm policy requires strict isolation. Be mindful of extensions. Only install what you absolutely need for your workflow. Every extension is a potential security hole. Periodically review your installed list and remove anything that is not actively used for your case work.

faq.question: Can I use Chrome extensions for eDiscovery?
faq.answer: Yes, but be careful. Only use extensions provided or vetted by your firm's IT department. Unauthorized extensions can interfere with review platform scripts.

faq.question: Why does Chrome slow down during large document reviews?
faq.answer: Review platforms are heavy on JavaScript and memory. Chrome allocates memory per tab. If you have too many tabs open, or if your cache is bloated, performance will drop.

faq.question: How do I keep my personal and work browsing separate?
faq.answer: Use Chrome Profiles. Create a separate profile for each client or matter. This keeps your history, bookmarks, and logins completely isolated.
